profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a university hospital between the clinical lead and the evidence-synthesis coordinator for a grant-funded follow-on project that will adapt findings from a systematic review on interdisciplinary bedside rounds (IBRs) into a multi-site implementation package. The team is preparing a shared evidence brief and site-readiness summary for three inpatient units before a steering committee review next week. The agenda is to align on what counts as an 'IBR' in the summary tables, confirm which study set and extraction sheet version will feed the implementation brief, clarify the handoff for feasibility barriers and patient-centeredness examples, and confirm what 'ready for committee' means for the shared materials. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on who will finalize the evidence brief, which materials will be circulated, and how the two workstreams will hand off their sections by Friday.

members.name: Dr. Lena Verhoeven
members.expertise: Interprofessional inpatient workflows, bedside rounding redesign, clinician engagement
members.background: A hospitalist who has led nursing-physician bedside rounding pilots on medical wards and now co-leads the translational phase of a review-informed implementation project.
members.private_state: She wants the committee packet to feel operationally actionable for unit leaders, avoid reopening conceptual debates about terminology, and keep the timeline intact despite incomplete site feedback.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'IBR definition,' the practical minimum is concurrent bedside participation by at least two professions plus the patient, even if families are not consistently included.
The 'master extraction sheet' is the cleaned implementation workbook circulated after last Tuesday's methods huddle, not the earlier review dataset used during article screening.
A section is 'ready for committee' once the narrative and examples are stable enough for leadership discussion, even if citation formatting and some risk-of-bias fields are still pending.
Feasibility barriers belong in the implementation brief only insofar as they affect ward workflow during rounds, not broader research-design limitations.

members.name: Sophie Marquez
members.expertise: Systematic reviews, qualitative evidence integration, study extraction governance
members.background: A senior research coordinator with training in epidemiology who managed article screening, data extraction, and quality appraisal for the systematic review and now supports the implementation package.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve methodological consistency with the published review, prevent drift in terminology across deliverables, and avoid presenting partially verified synthesis outputs as finalized evidence.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'IBR definition,' it should preserve the review's conceptual distinction among multidisciplinary rounds, interdisciplinary bedside rounds, and family-centered rounds, rather than collapsing them for operational convenience.
The 'master extraction sheet' is the locked review database on the shared drive that contains adjudicated study-level fields and tracked provenance, not any downstream implementation copy.
A section is 'ready for committee' only when references, study counts, quotations, and quality-appraisal links are fully reconciled so that no committee member sees an unstable evidence claim.

Feasibility barriers should include both bedside workflow issues and study-reported structural barriers such as hierarchy, role ambiguity, and definitional variability, because those are part of the evidence base.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'use the IBR definition from the review' in the summary tables.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a pragmatic operational definition for hospital units: bedside rounds with multiple professions present and patient participation, broad enough to support implementation examples across sites.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the review's conceptually differentiated definitions, where studies are kept distinct if they vary in patient involvement, family presence, or whether interaction is merely multidisciplinary versus genuinely interdisciplinary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are sincerely invoking the same review and the phrase 'use the review definition' sounds methodologically safe, neither expects the other to mean a different level of conceptual granularity.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'master extraction sheet' is the source of truth
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to updating 'the master extraction sheet' before circulating materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the implementation workbook revised last Tuesday that reorganizes findings into patient-centeredness, quality, collaboration, and feasibility tabs for committee consumption.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the locked adjudicated review spreadsheet on the shared drive containing the original 33-study extraction fields and audit trail.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are commonly called the master sheet within adjacent workstreams, and because each was recently updated and partially overlaps in content, the phrase feels unambiguous in context.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the evidence brief should be 'ready for committee by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the slide deck and summary memo are substantively complete enough to support steering discussion and site planning, even if some citations, exact counts, or appraisal annotations are finalized afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means every evidence statement in the packet is fully reconciled to the extraction source, references are verified, and no unresolved wording remains that could imply stronger certainty than the review supports.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital project meetings, 'ready' often functions as a routine deadline phrase, so both hear a normal coordination target rather than a cue to spell out different quality thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'feasibility section'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss folding the 'feasibility barriers' into one shared section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes barriers that unit leaders can directly act on during bedside rounds, such as timing, staffing overlap, and who needs to be present at the bedside.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the full evidence-based feasibility landscape, including hierarchy, lack of shared goals, varied responsibilities, conceptual inconsistency in IBR definitions, and other structural constraints reported across studies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are talking about feasibility from the same review, the category appears naturally shared, while the difference in practical versus comprehensive scope remains tacit.

turns.inner_thought: I need this meeting to lock the packet without reopening terminology debates. The steering group needs something operational, and I cannot let incomplete site feedback stall us. If the evidence brief and site-readiness summary are substantively stable, that's ready for committee by Friday, even if a few references or appraisal details get cleaned up afterward.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to make sure the evidence brief, the site-readiness summary, and the handoffs are all lined up so the IBR packet is ready for committee by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: I can finish my part, but only if we stay anchored to the published review language. When we say use the IBR definition from the review, that means preserving the distinctions we coded during synthesis, not flattening study differences for convenience. I also do not want anything to look finalized if the evidence statements are still drifting.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works from my side. I can finalize the evidence piece as long as we use the IBR definition from the review consistently across the tables and the narrative.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. The unit leads do not need nuanced taxonomy; they need one usable frame they can recognize across sites. For implementation, the practical floor is bedside participation by more than one profession with the patient there, and that should be enough to keep the examples coherent.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. Consistent wording is exactly what the unit leads need, and I think it will help if we keep one practical IBR definition across all three sites for clarity.

turns.inner_thought: I should update the locked review database today so the examples in the brief match the adjudicated study fields and provenance. If patient-centeredness and collaboration excerpts get copied from anything else, we risk introducing wording that is not traceable back to the review dataset.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll update the master extraction sheet today so the patient-centeredness and team-collaboration examples stay aligned with the reviewed studies.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's talking about the workbook we restructured on Tuesday. I need those implementation tabs current so I can pull directly into the memo without reworking everything. If the patient-centeredness, quality, collaboration, and feasibility tabs are refreshed, I can move quickly.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Can you make sure the master extraction sheet also reflects the implementation tabs from last Tuesday? That way I can lift content directly into the committee memo.

turns.inner_thought: Next I should consolidate the barriers reported across studies into one evidence-based section. Feasibility includes workflow, but also hierarchy, role confusion, structural constraints, and conceptual inconsistency because those affect uptake and were repeatedly coded in the literature.
turns.utterance: Yes. On the feasibility section, I'll consolidate the reported barriers so the packet captures what affects uptake of bedside rounds.

turns.inner_thought: As long as that section stays concise and useful for the steering group. They need barriers they can actually act on in ward operations: timing, staffing overlap, and who needs to be at the bedside. I don't want a long methods-style discussion of everything studies found.
turns.utterance: That sounds right. For the steering group, I think a concise feasibility section focused on time, bedside workflow, and getting the right people in the room should be enough.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep it concise, but I am definitely retaining the broader barriers from the review. Hierarchy, role ambiguity, and differences in definitions were prominent and they matter if we're claiming to summarize feasibility faithfully. Those issues also reinforce why the IBR definition from the review has to stay intact.
turns.utterance: I can do that, and I'll also preserve the evidence on hierarchy, role ambiguity, and differences in definitions because those were important barriers reported across studies.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, as long as it doesn't derail the packet. What I need by Friday is a stable brief for leadership discussion: clear summary, a few good examples, and recommendations the sites can react to. We can polish citations and residual evidence mechanics after the committee if needed.
turns.utterance: That works. For me, ready for committee by Friday mainly means we have a stable summary, a few illustrative examples, and clean recommendations for the sites.

turns.inner_thought: I need to say this plainly enough to protect the evidence standards without sounding obstructive. Friday is fine, but only if every claim is reconciled first. Ready for committee by Friday means references verified, study counts checked, and appraisal links consistent so nothing unstable gets in front of the steering group.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll aim for Friday as long as the citations, study counts, and appraisal links are fully reconciled before anything goes into the packet.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll move the committee memo as soon as she sends the updated workbook and the feasibility wording. Once the Tuesday implementation tabs are refreshed, I can assemble something leadership-ready quickly and keep the timeline intact.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll draft the committee-facing memo once you send the updated master sheet and the feasibility language.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the locked extraction file updates and the review-based definitions later today, then finish reconciliation so Friday's version is truly committee-ready. I assume Lena just wants the current evidence package built from the same source of truth and terminology we've been using.
